doc.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021

chapter: Studio work, recordings and Saturday Night Live
title: What studio work really was for him
summary: Turré says he rarely did jingle or sight-reading studio work; his sessions were jazz record dates where you learn the music and listen to each other.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: I feel like I’m getting a terrific lesson here today, Steve.
You asked, I’m telling you my experiences, you know?

Yes indeed. So as your career went on you found ways not only to have meaningful musical experiences but to make a living. And you did a good amount of studio work. Can you take us through a typical day of a studio musician from getting a phone call to showing up and how that worked and what it required?

Well I’ll set the record straight here. What most people think of as a studio musician would be like somebody that does jingles and does movie scores and goes in and sight reads parts for background horn parts for a record date for a pop singer or whoever, something like that. I never was into that scene. Never. I might have done about what you can count on one hand that kind of work. But I did a lot of jazz record dates, which is a totally different experience. Totally different. It’s not about whether you could sight read, it was about whether you could play. You get the music, you go home, you do your

homework, you learn it, you have a rehearsal, and then you go in the studio and you play. You’ve got to listen and not just listen for what, you know, the click track or you know that kind of thing. You listen to each other in an organic way. You respond to the moment.
